title: F. Familiar?
statement:
Note the unusual memory limit.

Consider the following pseudocode that processes a permutation $$p$$ of length $$n$$$$^{∗}$$:

You are given an array $$a$$ of length $$n$$. Your task is to count the number of permutations $$p$$ of length $$n$$ such that, if $$b$$ is the array returned by mystery(p) , the condition $$a_i = b_i$$ holds for all $$i$$ ($$1 $\leq i \leq n$$$) where $$a_i $\neq -1$$$.

Since the answer can be very large, output it modulo $$998\,244\,353$$.

$$^{∗}$$A permutation of length $$n$$ is an array consisting of $$n$$ distinct integers from $$1$$ to $$n$$ in arbitrary order. For example, $$[2,3,1,5,4]$$ is a permutation, but $$[1,2,2]$$ is not a permutation ($$2$$ appears twice in the array), and $$[1,3,4]$$ is also not a permutation ($$n=3$$ but there is $$4$$ in the array).

Each test contains multiple test cases. The first line contains the number of test cases $$t$$ ($$1 $\leq t \leq 10^4$$$). The description of the test cases follows.

The first line of each test case contains an integer $$n$$ ($$1 $\leq n \leq 500$$$), representing the length of $$a$$.

The second line contains $$n$$ integers $$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$ ($$-1 $\leq a_i \leq n$$$), representing the elements in $$a$$.

It is guaranteed that the sum of $$n^3$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$500^3$$.

For each test case, output an integer representing the number of permutations, modulo $$998\,244\,353$$.

In the first and second test cases, the only valid permutation is $$[1]$$.

In the fourth test case, the valid permutations are $$[1,2,4,3]$$, $$[3,4,2,1]$$, and $$[1,4,3,2]$$.

In the fifth test case, all permutations of length $$6$$ are valid.

The second line contains $$n$$ integers $$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_n$$ ($$-1 $\leq a_i \leq n$$$), representing the elements in $$a$$. It is guaranteed that the sum of $$n^3$$ over all test cases does not exceed $$500^3$$.
output: Output For each test case, output an integer representing the number of permutations, modulo $$998\,244\,353$$.
